historical_timeline.summary: Began ballet training with Lubov Egorova, almost eight hours a day.
First breakdown; hospitalized for nervous exhaustion.
Admitted to Les Rives de Prangins, Nyon; treated for schizophrenia until September 1931.
Entered the Phipps Clinic, Johns Hopkins.
Returned to Sheppard Pratt from Craig House.
Died in a fire at Highland Hospital.

claims.statement: Zelda Sayre was born on July 24, 1900, in Montgomery, Alabama, the youngest child of Alabama Supreme Court Justice Anthony Dickson Sayre and Minnie Buckner Machen Sayre; as a girl she starred in ballet recitals.
In July 1918 she met F. Scott Fitzgerald; they married in New York on April 3, 1920, and their only child, Frances "Scottie" Fitzgerald, was born in 1921.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history as context only; the modern episode gives no role to her husband or daughter.

claims.statement: In the late 1920s she returned to dance. She began ballet lessons at 27 with Lubov Egorova, hoping to dance with the Ballets Russes, and took classes every morning and afternoon, practising for almost eight hours a day.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern dance training, the eating and exercise screen, and the amenorrhea.

source_links.locator: returned to two childhood passions, art and dance

claims.statement: In 1930 the stress of her frustrated attempts to become a professional ballerina led to the first of many breakdowns. On a trip to Europe that year she was hospitalized for nervous exhaustion.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic first episode of psychosis and its index age.

claims.statement: From June 1930 to September 1931 she lived at the Les Rives de Prangins clinic in Nyon, Switzerland, where she was treated for schizophrenia; her main physician was Dr. Oscar Forel. She was diagnosed as schizophrenic in 1930 and gave up ballet.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

source_links.locator: diagnosed as schizophrenic later in 1930, when she retired from ballet

claims.statement: In February 1932 she entered the Phipps Clinic of Johns Hopkins University, where she completed her only novel, Save Me the Waltz.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; her writing in hospital is recorded as a strength.

source_links.locator: wrote her only published novel in hospital in 1932

claims.statement: By 1934 she was spending her weekdays in the Sheppard and Enoch Pratt Hospital in Towson, Maryland. After a brief period of wellness her illness worsened; she was moved to Craig House in New York and returned to Sheppard Pratt in May 1934.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: In April 1936 she moved to Highland Hospital in Asheville, North Carolina, where she lived until 1940; afterwards she returned there at times when depression became debilitating, and her stays were intermittent until her death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date; recorded as history.

claims.statement: She wrote and painted throughout her life; a 1934 exhibition in New York showed her paintings and drawings.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her creative work is recorded as a strength.

claims.statement: Late on the night of March 10, 1948, a fire that started in a kitchen of the main building of Highland Hospital spread through the building; nine patients died, among them Zelda Fitzgerald.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only, recorded without detail. One source dates the fire to the night of March 10 to 11.

claims.statement: Although she was treated for schizophrenia, mental-health experts later contested both the diagnosis and the treatment prescribed by her main physician.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective; the reason the modern diagnosis begins as provisional.

claims.statement: A psychiatrist writing to the Princeton Alumni Weekly argued that her history of remissions and exacerbations makes schizophrenia highly unlikely and bipolar illness more likely.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective opinion in a reader's letter; puts bipolar I disorder first in the modern differential.

claims.statement: The psychiatrist Mary Seeman, drawing on biographies, describes her illness as showing specific precipitants, discontinuities in its course, pronounced mood swings, preserved intellect and agency, and flare-ups associated with immune and hormonal changes, as an example of how psychosis can present in women.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; supports attention to mood, hormonal change and course in the modern episode.

claims.statement: Her ballet training has been described as an obsession bordering on mania. The project roster reads it as an exercise compulsion with an eating disorder, an interpretation that no fetched clinical source makes.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective; the reason the modern episode screens for disordered eating and compulsive exercise without assuming either.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Dignified, recovery-oriented primary care for a 29-year-old dancer and writer twelve days after a first psychiatric admission for psychosis with marked manic and depressive symptoms: holding the diagnosis provisional (bipolar I disorder with psychotic features, schizoaffective disorder, or schizophreniform disorder or schizophrenia) and showing how the course settles it; lithium with level, kidney, thyroid and calcium monitoring and sick-day rules learned from a lithium level above range during gastroenteritis; antipsychotic metabolic and prolactin monitoring, with a switch from risperidone to aripiprazole when raised prolactin and amenorrhea persisted; reproductive health on teratogenic medicines (valproate avoided, contraception and folic acid); an eating and exercise screen for a dancer with low weight and missed periods; coordinated specialty care; and a structured safety assessment with lethal-means counseling and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline reviewed at every visit, on the CANMAT and ISBD bipolar guidelines, the APA 1924 schizophrenia guideline, and the CMID depression and bipolar monograph.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Fitzgerald returns one week after her first visit and is seen by Dr. Langford of the coordinated specialty care team on the same day. She takes risperidone 2 mg every night. She sleeps nine or ten hours and feels heavy and slow in the mornings. She has had no voices, no sense of being watched, and no racing thoughts. Her mood is still low but less tearful, and she has begun writing again for an hour a day. Her periods have still not returned; she has had no breast discharge. She is eating three small meals and has not danced. She is worried that medicines will make her gain weight and end her dancing. She has had no thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

Dr. Langford agrees that the history points most strongly to bipolar I disorder with psychotic features but that the order of the mood and psychotic symptoms is not yet clear, so the diagnosis stays provisional. To prevent another episode she advises lithium, the first choice for long-term prevention. assessment.assessment: The full manic syndrome before admission and the depressive phase after it make bipolar I disorder with psychotic features the most likely diagnosis. Schizoaffective disorder would require psychotic symptoms for two weeks or more without mood symptoms, and schizophrenia would require psychosis outside mood episodes and usually a decline in function; neither is shown, but the order of symptoms is not yet established. A clearer history, from her own notes or journal and, with her consent, from her roommate, together with the course over the next months, should settle it; the diagnosis should be reviewed at about three months and again if psychosis ever occurs without mood symptoms. Lithium is the first choice for preventing further episodes. Valproate should not be used in a woman who could become pregnant because of its risks of birth defects and effects on a child's development. Lithium carries a small added risk of heart defects with exposure early in pregnancy, which is manageable with reliable contraception and planned pregnancy

The periods stopped before risperidone, which points to low energy availability from heavy training at a low weight; risperidone's prolactin rise may now be prolonging it. Changing the antipsychotic and adding lithium at the same time would make side effects hard to read, so lithium should be started first and the antipsychotic switched if prolactin stays high and the periods do not return

recommendations: Start lithium carbonate 300 mg twice daily now; check a 12-hour trough level 5 to 7 days after starting and after any change, aiming for 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L
Creatinine and eGFR every two to three months for six months, TSH once or twice in the first six months, calcium yearly, then lithium level every three to six months
Teach and write down lithium sick-day rules: stop it during vomiting, diarrhea, or dehydration and call; avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers
Do not use valproate. Use reliable contraception, preferably a long-acting method, and plan any pregnancy with psychiatry
Continue risperidone for now; if prolactin is still raised and her periods have not returned at the next check, switch to aripiprazole, which spares prolactin and has a lower metabolic risk

Monitor weight at every visit for six months after starting or changing the antipsychotic, blood pressure, fasting glucose or A1c and lipids at 12 weeks to four months and then yearly, and the AIMS every six months

Continue lithium for the long term after a first manic episode with psychosis; consider a slow taper of the antipsychotic after six months or more of remission, with a written relapse plan
